questions.question: Who was the Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate when the Bahmani Kingdom was established in South India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq​**

 
 
• Jauna Khan succeeded his father in AD 1325 under the title of Muhammad- bin-Tughlaq.
 
• He was the most learned scholar of his time and knew both Arabic and Persian and had a comprehensive knowledge of philosophy, astronomy, logic, mathematics, and physical science.
 
• The Sultan maintained good relationships with foreigners and received an envoy from the Chinese ruler.
 
• Toghan Timur (AD 1341), who came to seek permission to rebuild Buddhist Monasteries, in the Himalayan region which was destroyed during the crucial expedition.
 
• The sultan gave permission and sent Ibn Battuta to the court of the Chinese emperor in 1347.
 
• Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Morocco. He came to India in 1333 and was appointed as the chief Qazi of Delhi by Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Shamsud-Din Iltutmish**

 
 
• He was a slave of Qutubuddin Aibak and occupied the throne of Delhi in 1211 AD after deposing Aram Bakhsh.
 
• He regarded as the ‘real founder of the Slave Dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate’ because he freed the Delhi Sultanate from the claim of suzerainty by the rulers of Ghazni.
 
• He made Delhi the capital in place of Lahore.
 
• He saved Delhi Sultanate from the wrath of Changez Khan by refusing shelter to Khwarizm Shah, whom Changez Khan was chasing.
 
• He got his authority (Sultanate of Delhi) recognised by the Caliph of Baghdad (Khalifa) as a member of the world fraternity of Islamic states.
 
• He completed the construction of Qutub Minar.
 
• He constituted a group of 40 nobles known as* Turkan-i-Chahalgani or Chalisa.*
 
• He started the Iqta-dar system in Delhi Sultanate. This is an assignment of land in lieu of salary, which he distributed to his officers.
 
• He introduced the silver coin (tanka) and the copper coin (jital).
 
• He patronised Minhaj-al-Siraj, author of *Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.*
 
 

 
• **​Ibrahim Lodi ** 

 
 
• Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty, ascended the throne in 1517 after the death of his father, Sikandar Lodi. His reign, however, was marked by a series of challenges and internal conflicts.
 
• Lodi's impulsive and tyrannical nature alienated many of his nobles, leading to widespread discontent and rebellion. His harsh policies and disregard for the concerns of his subjects further eroded his support base.
 
• The internal turmoil within the Lodi Sultanate provided an opportunity for external forces to exploit the situation. Babur, the ruler of Kabul, saw this as an opportune moment to invade India.
 
• In 1526, the decisive Battle of Panipat took place, where Babur's small but well-disciplined army, equipped with superior artillery, defeated Ibrahim Lodi's larger but disorganized forces.
 
• Ibrahim Lodi's defeat and death marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India. His reign serves as a cautionary tale about the importance of effective leadership and the consequences of internal divisions.
 
 
 
• **Alauddin Khalji****​**
 
• Alauddin Khalji was an emperor of the Khalji dynasty.
 
 
• Alauddin was a nephew and son-in-law of the Jalaluddin Khalji, founder of the Khalji dynasty.
 
• He ruled the Delhi Sultanate in 1296–1316.
 
• He adopted the title "Sikander-i-Sani.".
 
• He adopted the Blood and Iron policy of Balban in tackling the Mongols.
 
• Introduced Chehra and Dagh system.
 
• Alauddin built the Siri Fort, The Hauz-i-Khas, Alai Darwaza.
 
 
 
• The Jamat Khana Masjid is the mosque in Delhi built by Khizr Khan.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution?

A. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 added six Directive Principles of State Policy to the Constitution.

B. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 substituted a new article for Article 45 and made elementary education as a Fundamental Right.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), outlined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution (Articles 36-51), are non-justiciable in nature.
 
• This means that they are not enforceable by any court.
 
• However, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the state to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• The DPSP, though not enforceable, serve as a guide to the legislative and executive branches of the government when they create policies and laws.
 
• They aim to establish a welfare state where justice and equality are prevalent.
 
• Despite their non-justiciable nature, the principles hold significant influence on the interpretation of the Constitution and the legislation.
 
• This is because they reflect the ambitions and values that the Constitution strives to uphold.
 
• Please note that while these principles are not enforceable by courts, they significantly shape India's governance and legal discourse.
 
• The Constitution itself declares that it is the responsibility of the State to apply these principles in law-making and policy design.
 
• 
 
This provides them with a considerable indirect impact on legislation and governance.

questions.question: Magma is defined as:

options.text: the extremely hot liquid and semi-liquid rock located under the Earth's surface
the extremely hot solid core of the Earth
the volatile gaseous environment under the Earth’s surface
the extremely hot water springs of the Atlantic region

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the extremely hot liquid and semi-liquid rock located under the Earth's surface**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

Igneous Rocks are formed by crystallization from a liquid or magma. Magma is a mixture of liquid rock, crystals, and gas with a wide range of chemical compositions, temperatures, and properties of a liquid.

There are two types of Igneous rocks based on their mode of occurrence:

 
• Volcanic or extrusive igneous rocks that form when the magma cools and crystallizes on the surface of the Earth
 
• Intrusive or plutonic igneous rocks wherein the magma crystallizes at depth in the Earth.

Extrusive igneous rocks

 
• As lava cools very rapidly on coming out of the hot interior of the earth, the mineral crystals forming these rocks are very fine.
 
• These rocks are also called volcanic rocks. Basalt is a very common example of such rocks.
 
• These rocks are found in volcanic areas.
 
• Deccan plateau’s regur soil in India is a formation of lava.

Intrusive igneous rocks

 
• The rate of cooling below the earth’s surface is very slow, which gives rise to the formation of large crystals in the rocks.
 
• Deep-seated intrusive rocks are termed as plutonic rocks and shallow depth intrusive rocks are termed as hypabyssal. Granite is a common example of intrusive rocks.

President

 
• The President is the head of the Indian State. He is India's first citizen and serves as a symbol of the country's unity, integrity, and solidarity.
 
• He is a part of the Union Executive, the provisions of which are addressed in Articles 52-78, including articles concerning the President (Articles 52-62).
 
• Election of President
 
 
• There is no direct election for the Indian President. An electoral college elects him. The electoral college responsible for President’s elections comprises elected members of:
 
 
• Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
 
• Legislative Assemblies of the states (Legislative Councils have no role)
 
• Legislative Assemblies of the Union Territories of Delhi, Puducherry, Kashmir, Ladakh.

• Nominated Members of State Legislative Assemblies
 
• Members of Legislative Councils (Both elected and nominated) in bicameral legislatures
 
• Nominated Members of union territories of Delhi and Puducherry, Kashmir, and Ladakh.
 
 
 
• Impeachment
 
 
• The President can be removed from office by impeachment for "constitutional violations." However, the word "violation of the Constitution" is not defined in the Constitution.
 
• Article 61 of the Constitution of India prescribes the procedure for the impeachment of the President.
 
• The impeachment process can be started from any house of the parliament by leveling charges against him.
 
• The notice bearing the charges against the president must be signed by at least a quarter of the members of the house.

 The resolution to impeach the president must be passed by a special majority (two-thirds) in the originating house.
 
• Next, it is sent to the other house for consideration. The other house acts as the investigating horse. A select committee is formed to investigate the charges labeled against the president.
 
• There is no provision for the suspension of the President during the period of Impeachment.
 
• During the process, the President of India has the right to defend himself through authorized counsel. He can choose to defend himself or appoint any person/lawyer or attorney general of India to do so.

• Conversely, low population density may indicate underutilization of resources and potentially lesser economic development.

questions.question:
Identify the correct statement in the context of National Income Accounting.

(i) Depreciation is unexpected obsolescence.

(ii) Capital loss is unexpected obsolescence.

(iii) Intermediate goods get completely used up or are resold during a given year.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only (ii)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• National income accounting

 
 
• It is a bookkeeping method used by governments to track the level of economic activity in their country through time. 
 
• Total revenues made by domestic firms, wages given to foreign and domestic workers, and the amount spent on sales and income taxes by corporations and individuals resident in the nation are all examples of accounting records of this type. 
 
• National Income
 
 
• After depreciation, the total worth of final products and services generated by normal residents throughout an accounting year is called the national income. 
 
• It is Net National Product (NNP) At Factor Cost (FC).
 
• Taxes, depreciation, and non-factor inputs are not included (raw materials).
 
 
 
• Domestic Income 
 
 
• After depreciation, the total worth of final products and services generated inside a domestic area within an accounting year is called domestic income. 
 
• It is NDP (National Domestic Product) at Factor Cost.
 
• NNP and NDP may be calculated using either constant prices (real income) or market prices (nominal income).
 
• Domestic income plus net factor income from abroad (NFIA) equals national income.
 
 
 
• Although national income accounting is not an exact science, it does give important information about how well an economy is performing and where money is created and spent. 
 
• Data on per capita income and growth may be evaluated across time when paired with statistics on the corresponding population.
 
• The gross domestic product (GDP), gross national product (GNP), and gross national income (GNI) are some of the indicators computed using national income accounting.
 
• The GDP is a frequently used metric for domestic economic research, and it reflects the total market value of goods and services produced in a certain country during a given period of time.
